title: The Shipbuilder's Apprentice
summary: A boy named Yusuf, apprenticed to a master dhow-builder on the Red Sea coast, helps solve a tricky design problem when an unusual commission makes the usual boat shape unsafe.
poll: A master craftsperson should always stick to tried-and-true methods instead of trying new ideas.

versions.title: The Shipbuilder's Apprentice
versions.text:
Yusuf is a boy. He lives by the sea. He helps Hamid. Hamid builds boats. He makes big wooden boats. They are dhows.

Yusuf is an apprentice. He is learning to build boats. He cuts wood. He shapes it. He watches Hamid work.

One day, a man comes to the shop. His name is Faris. He wants a new boat. It must carry heavy stone. It must be fast, too.

Hamid builds the boat. He uses his old way. But something is wrong! The boat sits too low. It tips to one side.

Yusuf has an idea. He saw a fishing boat once. It had a wide bottom. It did not tip. He tells Hamid his idea.

Hamid tries a new shape. The bottom is wide. It works! The boat floats well. It is fast, too. Faris is glad. Hamid is proud of him.

Hamid tries a new shape for the boat. He makes the bottom wide and round. It works! The boat floats well and sails fast, too. Faris is delighted, and Hamid feels proud of him.

Yusuf is a boy who lives by the sea, in a small coastal town. He helps Hamid, a master boat builder. Hamid builds large wooden boats called dhows.

Yusuf is Hamid's apprentice. He is learning the craft of boat building, step by step. He cuts and shapes pieces of wood with care. He watches closely whenever Hamid tries something new.

One day, a wealthy merchant comes to the shop. His name is Faris. He wants a brand new boat that can carry heavy stone. The boat must still sail fast enough to beat the wind.

Hamid builds the boat using his usual design. But something goes wrong at the first test on the water. The boat sits too low. It tips dangerously to one side.

versions.title: The Shipbuilder's Apprentice
versions.text:
Yusuf is a boy who lives in the coastal town of Marsa Nakheel, on the Red Sea. For two years, he has worked as an apprentice to Hamid. Hamid is a master craftsman who builds large wooden boats called dhows.

Learning this craft takes patience. Yusuf has learned to choose strong, flexible wood. He shapes curved planks by bending them over a fire. He fits each plank snugly to form a sturdy hull. He watches closely whenever Hamid shows him a new step.

One day, a wealthy merchant named Faris arrives with an unusual commission. He wants a new dhow that can carry a heavy cargo of building stone. The boat must still sail quickly enough to reach a distant port.

Hamid builds the hull using his usual design, narrow and curved for speed. During the first test on the water, something goes wrong. Loaded with the heavy stone, the boat sits too low. It loses its balance and tips to one side.

Yusuf recalls something he once noticed in the harbor. A heavily loaded fishing boat with a wider hull floated steadily and kept its balance. It was slower, though, than a narrow boat. Yusuf shares this with Hamid.

Together, they build a small test model with a wider curve along the bottom of the hull. They float the model and load it with weights. It holds its balance perfectly.

Hamid reshapes the real dhow's hull, giving it a wider curve near the bottom while keeping the sides curved for speed. Tested again with the full cargo, the boat floats evenly and sails fast. Faris is delighted, and Hamid proudly credits his apprentice's sharp eye.

versions.title: The Shipbuilder's Apprentice
versions.text:
Yusuf is a boy who lives in the coastal town of Marsa Nakheel, on the Red Sea. For two years, he has worked as an apprentice to Hamid, a respected master craftsman who builds large wooden boats called dhows, vessels famous along the coast for their graceful curved hulls and old construction methods.

Learning this traditional craft requires patience and careful attention. Yusuf has learned to choose strong, flexible wood. He shapes curved planks by soaking and bending them over a fire until they take the right form. He fits each plank snugly against the next so the hull stays sturdy and watertight. He watches closely whenever Hamid shows him a new step, eager to understand why each step matters.

One day, a wealthy merchant named Faris arrives at the workshop with an unusual commission. He wants a new dhow capable of carrying a heavy cargo of building stone for a project farther down the coast. The boat must still sail quickly enough to reach a distant port before the winds change.

Hamid builds the hull using his usual design, narrow and deeply curved for speed, a shape that has served him well for many years. During the first test on the water, something goes wrong. Loaded with the heavy stone, the boat sits too low and loses its balance, tipping to one side instead of riding evenly.

Yusuf recalls something he once noticed down at the harbor. A heavily loaded fishing boat with a wider, flatter hull floated steadily and kept its balance even with a full catch. It moved somewhat slower, though, than a narrower boat would. Yusuf shares this observation with Hamid, wondering if a similar shape might help.

Together, they decide to build a small test model with a wider curve along the bottom of its hull, hoping to combine stability with reasonable speed. They float the model in a shallow pool and load it with weights to mimic the stone. It holds its balance perfectly.

Encouraged by this success, Hamid carefully reshapes the real dhow's hull, giving it a wider, gentler curve near the bottom while still keeping its sides curved for speed higher up. When the boat is tested again with the full cargo of stone aboard, it floats evenly and sails swiftly across the harbor. Faris is delighted with the result, and Hamid proudly tells everyone that it was his young apprentice's sharp eye that solved the problem.

versions.text:
Yusuf is a boy who lives in the coastal town of Marsa Nakheel, on the Red Sea. For two years, he has served as an apprentice to Hamid, a respected master craftsman who builds large wooden vessels called dhows, boats famous along the coast for their graceful curved hulls.

Mastering this traditional craft demands considerable patience and meticulous attention to detail. Yusuf has learned to select strong, flexible wood. He shapes curved planks by soaking and gradually bending them over a fire until they assume exactly the right form. He fits each plank snugly against the keel and its neighboring plank, sealing every seam with caulk so the finished hull remains sturdy and watertight. He observes closely whenever Hamid demonstrates a new technique, eager to understand why each step matters.

One day, a wealthy merchant named Faris arrives at the workshop with an unusual commission. He requests a new dhow capable of transporting an unusually heavy cargo of building stone for a construction project farther down the coast, yet one that can still sail swiftly enough to reach the distant port before the seasonal winds shift direction.

Hamid constructs the hull according to his customary design, narrow and deeply curved for speed, a shape that has served him reliably for many years. During the initial test on the water, however, something goes wrong: once loaded with the heavy stone, the boat sits far too low and loses its stability, tipping precariously to one side rather than riding evenly.

Yusuf recalls something he once observed down at the harbor. A heavily loaded fishing boat with a wider, flatter hull possessed considerably greater buoyancy and retained its stability even with a full catch, though it moved somewhat more slowly than a narrower vessel would. Yusuf shares this careful observation with Hamid, wondering aloud whether a comparable shape might resolve their predicament.

Together, they decide to construct a small test model featuring a wider curve along the bottom of its hull, hoping to combine stability with reasonable speed. They float the model in a shallow tide pool and load it with weights to simulate the stone cargo, and it maintains its balance perfectly.

Encouraged by this success, Hamid carefully reshapes the real dhow's hull, giving it a wider, gentler curve near the bottom and keel while still preserving curved sides for speed higher up. When the boat is tested once more with the full cargo of stone aboard, it floats evenly and sails swiftly across the harbor, precisely as Faris had hoped. Faris is delighted with the outcome, and Hamid proudly announces to everyone in the workshop that it was his young apprentice's keen eye that ultimately solved the problem and fulfilled this demanding commission.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A long and exciting trip to a faraway island
A boy apprentice who helps solve a problem with a new boat's design
A hungry fisherman who sells fish at the busy market
An exciting race between two very fast sailing boats
questions.why: The story follows Yusuf as he helps Hamid fix a boat that tips because of its shape.

wrong.A: No one sails to an island in this story.
wrong.C: Faris is a merchant, not a fisherman selling fish.
wrong.D: There is no race between boats in this story.

questions.stem: What does Yusuf do to help Hamid in the shop?
options: He cuts and shapes pieces of wood
He writes letters for traveling merchants
He catches fish every single morning
He builds small houses by the shore
questions.why: The story says Yusuf cuts and shapes wood as he learns to build boats.

wrong.B: Yusuf does not write letters in the story.
wrong.C: The story does not say Yusuf fishes.
wrong.D: Yusuf helps build boats, not houses.

questions.stem: What does the merchant Faris want from Hamid?
options: A tiny boat that is only used for fishing
A boat that can carry heavy stone and still sail fast
A boat built completely out of shiny metal
A boat that is meant only for a fun race
questions.why: The story says Faris wants a new boat that can carry heavy stone yet still sail quickly.

wrong.A: Faris wants more than a small fishing boat.
wrong.C: The dhow is made of wood, not metal.
wrong.D: The boat is for carrying stone, not racing.

questions.stem: In the story, what does apprentice mean?
options: someone who only buys and sells old boats
someone who is learning a skilled job from a master
a special kind of wooden sailing boat
the owner of a busy shop by the sea
questions.why: Yusuf is Hamid's apprentice, meaning he is learning the skilled craft of building boats from him.

wrong.A: An apprentice learns a skill; he does not just trade boats.
wrong.C: Apprentice describes a person, not a boat.
wrong.D: Hamid, not Yusuf, owns the shop.

questions.stem: Why does the first boat tip to one side?
options: The wood was painted the wrong bright color
It is too heavy and not built the right shape for the load
Hamid forgot to add a tall sail to it
Yusuf did not help build that particular boat

wrong.C: The story does not mention a missing sail.
wrong.D: Yusuf helps build the boat from the start.

options: He simply wants to own a boat just like it one day
He dislikes the usual narrow shape that dhows are built in

wrong.C: Faris is pleased, not upset, with the boat.

keyWords.definition: the main body of a boat or ship that sits in the water
keyWords.example: Water slowly leaked into the old hull of the fishing boat.

keyWords.definition: a long, flat piece of wood used in building
keyWords.example: The workers nailed a new plank onto the wooden floor.

keyWords.definition: a steady position in which nothing tips over
keyWords.example: The gymnast kept her balance while walking on the beam.

keyWords.definition: goods that are carried by a ship, truck, or plane
keyWords.example: The truck delivered a heavy cargo of bricks to the site.

keyWords.definition: a line or shape that bends smoothly rather than being straight
keyWords.example: The road has a sharp curve near the old bridge.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Yusuf's careful observation of another boat helps Hamid solve a design problem and complete a difficult commission.
Dhows are described as being, without question, the fastest boats anywhere in the entire world.
Hamid is shown refusing completely to ever listen to his young apprentice's ideas.
Faris eventually decides, for no clear reason at all, not to buy a boat after all.
questions.why: The story centers on how Yusuf's memory of a wide-hulled fishing boat helps Hamid redesign the dhow successfully.

wrong.B: The story does not claim dhows are the fastest boats in the world.
wrong.C: Hamid listens to Yusuf and changes the design.
wrong.D: Faris is happy with the finished boat, not cancelling the order.

questions.stem: What problem occurs when Hamid builds the hull using his usual narrow, curved design?
options: The boat turns out to be far too expensive for Faris to afford
The boat loses its balance and tips when loaded with heavy cargo
The wood used for the hull splits badly in the hot sun
Faris suddenly changes his mind about the stone cargo
questions.why: The story explains that the narrow hull sits too low and tips once it is loaded with the heavy stone.

wrong.A: Cost is never mentioned as a problem in the story.
wrong.C: Splitting wood is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: Faris does not change his mind about the cargo.

questions.stem: What shape does Yusuf recall from the fishing boat at the harbor?
options: A narrow hull that sits very deep in the water
A hull made out of thick, heavy metal plates
A boat that, in fact, has no hull at all
A wider, flatter hull
questions.why: Yusuf remembers a fishing boat with a wider, flatter hull that stayed steady even when heavily loaded.

wrong.A: The fishing boat's hull is wide, not narrow and deep.
wrong.B: Dhows and fishing boats here are wooden, not metal.
wrong.C: Every boat needs some kind of hull to float.

questions.stem: In the passage, what does balance mean as it relates to the boat?
options: the total price that Faris paid for the finished boat
the total number of wooden planks used to build it
the boat's ability to stay steady and not tip over
how fast the wind happens to be blowing that day
questions.why: The passage uses balance to describe the boat's ability to stay steady in the water rather than tipping.

wrong.A: Balance is not about the boat's price.
wrong.B: Balance is not about counting planks.
wrong.D: Balance describes steadiness, not wind speed.

questions.stem: Why do Hamid and Yusuf first test a small model instead of changing the real dhow right away?
options: They simply do not have enough wood left to build the real boat
Faris specifically asked them to build him a small toy instead
It is required by a strict law in their coastal town
They want to check whether the new shape works before risking the real boat
questions.why: Testing a small model first lets Hamid and Yusuf check the new shape safely before changing the actual dhow.

wrong.A: Running out of wood is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Faris never asks for a toy boat.
wrong.C: No law about models is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: Why was the wider fishing boat somewhat slower than a narrow boat?
options: It happened to have no sails fitted to it at all
A wider, flatter hull trades some speed for greater stability
It was simply much older than most of the other boats
Fishermen always rowed it instead of ever sailing it
questions.why: The passage explains that a wider hull gives more stability but moves somewhat more slowly than a narrow one.

wrong.A: Sails are not mentioned as the reason for its speed.
wrong.C: Age is not given as a reason for its speed.
wrong.D: Rowing versus sailing is not discussed in the story.

questions.stem: How does the final dhow design compare to the original design?
options: It ends up being exactly identical to the original design
It is made narrower everywhere compared to the original design
It combines a wider curve near the bottom for balance with curved sides for speed
It completely removes the keel from the boat's hull
questions.why: The final design keeps curved sides for speed but widens the bottom curve for better balance.

wrong.A: The final design changes the bottom curve, so it is not identical.
wrong.B: The design becomes wider, not narrower, at the bottom.
wrong.D: The keel is not removed in the story.

questions.stem: How does the passage mainly organize the events of the story?
options: It follows the problem of the tipping boat, then the idea, the test, and the fix, in order
It simply lists, one after another, the ingredients needed for building any boat
It compares, point by point, five completely different kinds of boats
It describes, from birth to old age, the merchant Faris's entire life story
questions.why: The passage moves in order from the tipping problem, to Yusuf's idea, to the test model, to the successful fix.

wrong.B: The passage is not a list of building ingredients.
wrong.C: Only two boat shapes are really compared, not five.
wrong.D: The passage is not a biography of Faris.

MID.prompt: Explain how Yusuf's observation and the test model helped Hamid solve the design problem. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Yusuf's observation helped solve the problem.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Yusuf's careful observation helped solve the design problem in an important way. He remembered that a heavily loaded fishing boat with a wider, flatter hull stayed balanced, even though it was a little slower than a narrow boat. He shared this idea with Hamid, and together they built a small test model with a wider curve at the bottom to check if it would work. When the model held its balance perfectly, Hamid reshaped the real dhow's hull the same way, which let it carry the heavy cargo of stone without tipping.

keyWords.definition: the ability of an object to float and resist sinking in a liquid
keyWords.example: Cork has enough buoyancy to float easily on water.

keyWords.definition: the long, central piece along the bottom of a boat that gives it strength and shape
keyWords.example: Workers bolted a sturdy keel along the bottom of the new ship.

keyWords.definition: the quality of being steady and not easily tipped over or upset
keyWords.example: Wide tires give the cart much better stability on rough roads.

keyWords.definition: a request to make or build something special for someone
keyWords.example: The painter accepted a commission to create a mural for the school.

keyWords.definition: a material used to seal cracks or seams so that water cannot get through
keyWords.example: Fresh caulk around the window kept the rain from leaking in.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: Yusuf's attentive observation and willingness to question the usual design help Hamid solve a structural problem and fulfill a demanding commission.
Dhows are presented in the passage as having never once been successfully redesigned throughout all of history.
Faris is shown eventually canceling the entire commission out of sheer frustration with Hamid's work.
Buoyancy is described in the passage as having essentially no real effect on how any boat floats.
questions.why: The passage centers on how Yusuf's observation and Hamid's willingness to adapt solve the hull's stability problem.

wrong.B: The passage shows a dhow being successfully redesigned.
wrong.C: Faris is delighted with the outcome, not frustrated.
wrong.D: Buoyancy is central to why the wider hull works better.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does Yusuf learn to do when fitting planks?
options: Paint each plank a bright color before it is ever fitted into place
Nail the planks only loosely so they can later be removed easily
Fit each plank snugly against the keel and seal seams with caulk
Leave deliberate gaps between planks to allow for ventilation
questions.why: The passage states that Yusuf learns to fit each plank against the keel and seal every seam with caulk.

wrong.A: Painting planks is not mentioned in the passage.
wrong.B: Planks are fitted snugly, not loosely, in the passage.
wrong.D: Gaps for ventilation are not mentioned in the passage.

questions.stem: What specifically causes the original hull to lose its stability?
options: A sudden and violent storm that strikes while at sea
A crack that develops in the keel because of its old age
Faris unexpectedly changing the agreed delivery date
The heavy cargo of stone combined with the hull's narrow, deep shape
questions.why: The passage explains that the heavy stone cargo combined with the narrow, deeply curved hull causes the loss of stability.

wrong.A: No storm at sea is described in the passage.
wrong.B: A cracked keel is not mentioned in the passage.
wrong.C: Faris does not change the delivery date.

questions.stem: In the passage, buoyancy most nearly refers to —
options: the price that was agreed upon for the commission
a vessel's tendency to float and resist sinking
the speed at which a given boat is able to sail
the particular sound a hull makes in rough water
questions.why: The passage uses buoyancy to describe the wider hull's greater ability to float and resist sinking.

wrong.D: Buoyancy is not about sound.

questions.stem: Why does a wider, flatter hull provide greater stability than a narrow one, based on the passage?
options: It spreads the boat's weight over a broader surface, resisting tipping, even though it sacrifices some speed
It happens to be built from an entirely different type of wood altogether
It has no keel whatsoever fitted to it, so it simply cannot tip at all
It is described as carrying noticeably less cargo than a narrow hull would
questions.why: A wider hull spreads weight over a broader surface, which resists tipping, though it trades away some speed.

wrong.B: The passage does not say the wood type differs.
wrong.C: A wider hull still has a keel in the passage.
wrong.D: Cargo capacity is not reduced in the passage.

questions.stem: What does Hamid's willingness to change his usual design suggest about him?
options: He is, in truth, quite stubborn and refuses any new ideas whatsoever
He has, by this point, completely lost all trust in his own skills
He values craftsmanship but remains open to a better solution when evidence supports it
He clearly dislikes working closely with any apprentices at all
questions.why: Hamid's willingness to test and adopt Yusuf's idea shows he values skilled craftsmanship but stays open to better solutions.

wrong.A: Hamid is open to Yusuf's new idea.
wrong.B: Hamid still relies on his own expertise throughout.
wrong.D: Hamid values and praises his apprentice.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events is correct?
options: Hamid reshapes the hull first, then builds a test model, and only then does Faris arrive with his commission
The reshaped hull succeeds first, and only afterward does Faris arrive, with the original hull failing last
Yusuf proposes his idea well before Faris ever arrives with the commission at all
Faris arrives with the commission, the original hull fails its stability test, Yusuf proposes an idea, and the reshaped hull succeeds
questions.why: The true order is: Faris arrives with the commission, the original hull fails, Yusuf proposes his idea, and the reshaped hull succeeds.

wrong.A: The commission comes before any reshaping happens.
wrong.B: The original hull fails before the reshaped one succeeds, not after.
wrong.C: Yusuf's idea comes only after the hull first fails.

questions.stem: Why does the passage end by reflecting that 'genuine mastery... lies not merely in repeating familiar methods'?
options: To suggest that experienced craftsmen should ignore absolutely every new idea they encounter
To emphasize that true skill includes the humility to adapt traditional methods when circumstances demand it
To argue that long-standing tradition should always be abandoned completely without question
To explain, in passing, why Faris happened to pay extra for this particular commission
questions.why: This closing reflection emphasizes that true mastery includes the humility to adapt a trusted method when circumstances require it.

wrong.A: Hamid listens to a new idea rather than ignoring it.
wrong.C: The passage does not argue for abandoning tradition entirely.
wrong.D: Extra payment is not mentioned in the passage.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says a master craftsperson should always stick to tried-and-true methods instead of trying new ideas. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the passage.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the passage.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that a master craftsperson should always stick to tried-and-true methods instead of trying new ideas. Hamid's experience with Faris's commission shows why: his usual narrow hull design, though reliable for years, failed once the heavy cargo of stone was loaded aboard. Only by listening to Yusuf's observation about the wider fishing boat, and testing a small model to check the idea, was Hamid able to fix the problem and complete the commission successfully. Someone might argue that a master's long experience should be trusted over a young apprentice's suggestion, but the passage shows that genuine skill includes the humility to adapt an old design when the evidence clearly calls for it.
